text_basis.sblgnt_reading: Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας, ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός
text_basis.na28_alignment: The NA28 and UBS5 agree with the SBLGNT in reading τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός; no substantive deviation exists between SBLGNT and NA28/UBS5 for this verse, though the Sinaitic Syriac (sys) preserves a well-known variant involving Joseph's paternity that is noted in critical apparatuses.
text_basis.dispute_note: The verse is a noted locus of textual tension primarily because of the Sinaitic Syriac (sys) variant, which reads 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, begat Jesus who is called the Christ,' appearing to attribute physical begetting to Joseph. This variant has generated extensive discussion regarding its relationship to the virginal conception tradition and whether it represents an early independent witness or a secondary corruption.

alexandrian.note: The primary Alexandrian witnesses א and B firmly support the standard reading τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς, affirming Mary as the one from whom Jesus was born without assigning physical paternity to Joseph. This Alexandrian consensus carries substantial weight given the early date and general reliability of these witnesses in the Gospel tradition.

witnesses: sys (Sinaitic Syriac — technically Syriac but often cited alongside Western witnesses for early divergent readings)
western.note: The Sinaitic Syriac (sys), while not strictly a Western witness, introduces the most significant variant: 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, begat (ܐܘܠܕ) Jesus who is called the Christ,' which superficially implies Joseph's physical paternity. Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin manuscripts show minor orthographic or stylistic variations but do not diverge on the substantive theological point as dramatically as sys.

byzantine.note: The Byzantine tradition uniformly supports the standard reading and offers no distinctive variant at this point, presenting τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός in full agreement with the Alexandrian text. The Byzantine tradition's late medieval harmonizing tendencies are not a significant factor here since all major streams (except sys) converge on the same reading.

caesarean.note: Caesarean witnesses, where extant for this passage, do not preserve a distinctive Caesarean variant and align with the standard reading affirming Mary as the mother from whom Jesus was born. The Ferrar group (f13) and Family 1 offer no support for the sys variant and present the received text without notable divergence.

metzger_rating.justification: Metzger and the UBS committee assigned a rating reflecting near-certainty for the standard reading ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς but acknowledged the Sinaitic Syriac variant as a non-trivial problem requiring comment, which slightly depresses confidence below an 'A' rating. The overwhelming Greek manuscript tradition is unanimous in supporting the received text, but the age of the Sinaitic Syriac and the difficulty of explaining the origin of its variant introduce a degree of residual uncertainty. The committee concluded that the sys reading most likely reflects a scribal adaptation to harmonize the genealogical structure of Matthew 1:1–16 with the standard ἐγέννησεν formula used in vv. 2–15, rather than preserving an original tradition.

variant_register.variant_text: τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός (standard reading: 'the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus who is called Christ')
variant_register.manuscript_support: א, B, C, D (substantially), L, W, Z, f1, f13, Majority Text, TR, Vulgate, Peshitta, most versional evidence
variant_register.assessment: This reading is supported by the broadest and earliest attestation across all manuscript families and versions, making it the strongest candidate for the original text. The passive ἐγεννήθη ('was born') with Mary as the antecedent of the relative pronoun ἧς deliberately breaks the active ἐγέννησεν pattern of the preceding genealogy to signal the unique nature of Jesus' birth, a stylistic distinction that would be intrinsically motivated by the author.

variant_register.variant_text: Sinaitic Syriac (sys) variant: 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, begat Jesus who is called the Christ' (ܝܘܣܦ ܗܘ ܕܡܟܝܪܐ ܗܘܬ ܠܗ ܡܪܝܡ ܒܬܘܠܬܐ ܐܘܠܕ ܠܝܫܘܥ ܗܘ ܕܡܬܩܪܐ ܡܫܝܚܐ)
variant_register.manuscript_support: Sinaitic Syriac (sys, 4th–5th century palimpsest); possibly reflected in traces of the Curetonian Syriac (syc) and cited by some early commentators in harmonized forms
variant_register.assessment: The sys variant's use of the active 'begat' (ܐܘܠܕ) for Joseph superficially disrupts the virginal conception narrative and has been interpreted by some scholars (e.g., Burkitt) as preserving an archaic pre-theological tradition, but this view is now largely rejected. It is more plausibly explained as a Syriac scribe's mechanical extension of the genealogical ἐγέννησεν formula through verse 16, with the qualifying phrase 'the virgin' added to protect the theological point, making it a transcriptional harmonization rather than an original reading.

variant_register.variant_text: Curetonian Syriac (syc) reading: a slightly modified form approximating 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, she bore to him Jesus who is called the Christ' — a middle position between sys and the Greek
variant_register.manuscript_support: Curetonian Syriac (syc, 5th century); debated whether it independently attests the sys tradition or represents a partial correction toward the Greek
variant_register.assessment: The Curetonian Syriac at this verse is sometimes read as an intermediate form suggesting early Syriac manuscripts had not yet settled on the theologically precise passive construction, but most text critics regard it as derivative rather than representing an independent textual tradition that predates the Greek witnesses. Its agreement with the sys reading in attributing some active role to Joseph is best understood as a shared Syriac scribal tendency rather than an echo of a pre-canonical source.

variant_register.variant_text: Minor orthographic/nomina sacra variants: spelling of Ἰησοῦς, presence or absence of the movable ν in ἐγέννησεν, and minor itacistic variants in individual manuscripts
variant_register.manuscript_support: Scattered across various uncials and minuscules; no single major manuscript family exclusively
variant_register.assessment: These minor variants are purely orthographic and carry no theological or exegetical significance; they reflect normal scribal habits in Greek manuscript transmission and are universally regarded as non-original secondary adaptations. They do not affect the meaning of the text or the text-critical evaluation of the verse's substantive content.

synthesis: Matthew 1:16 is text-critically stable in its Greek tradition, with all major manuscript families — Alexandrian, Byzantine, and Caesarean — converging on the reading that identifies Joseph as the husband of Mary and names Mary alone as the one from whom Jesus was born, using the passive ἐγεννήθη to mark a deliberate departure from the genealogical formula of vv. 2–15. The only significant challenge comes from the Sinaitic Syriac, a versional witness that introduces an active construction attributing begetting to Joseph, but this variant is broadly rejected by contemporary scholarship as a secondary scribal harmonization rather than a window into an alternative early tradition. The verse therefore presents a high degree of textual certainty in the Greek tradition, with the residual uncertainty introduced by the sys variant keeping it from an unqualified 'A' rating in Metzger's methodology.

assessment.title: Matthew 1:16: Stable Greek Text Despite Sinaitic Syriac Variant Challenge
assessment.reasoning: The Greek manuscript tradition for Matthew 1:16 is essentially unanimous in its witness to the standard reading, with Alexandrian, Western (Greek), Byzantine, and Caesarean witnesses all supporting the passive construction ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς, which carefully distinguishes Jesus' birth from the active genealogical formula used for all preceding generations. The Sinaitic Syriac variant, while early and geographically significant, is best explained by internal evidence as a scribal effort to extend the genealogical ἐγέννησεν pattern uniformly through the list, with the insertion of 'virgin' functioning as a compensatory theological safeguard — a procedure more consistent with scribal harmonization than original authorship. Metzger's committee, following the canons of both external attestation breadth and internal stylistic analysis, correctly identified the passive Greek reading as original and the sys variant as secondary, a conclusion that has not been seriously challenged in critical scholarship since the early twentieth century debates around Burkitt's proposals. The verse's deliberate syntactic break at v. 16 — shifting from active ἐγέννησεν to the passive relative clause — is precisely the kind of literary signal Matthew employs to prepare for the virginal conception account in 1:18–25, providing strong intrinsic support for the received text.
assessment.plain: Almost every ancient Greek manuscript of Matthew's Gospel reads that Joseph was Mary's husband and that Jesus was born from Mary — not that Joseph fathered Jesus — and this reading is considered virtually certain by textual scholars. The only major exception is an old Syriac translation that seems to say Joseph 'begat' Jesus, but most scholars believe that scribe was simply following the pattern of the family list too mechanically and added the word 'virgin' to clarify he didn't mean it literally. The standard Greek text is firmly established and is printed in all modern critical editions of the New Testament.
assessment.recommended_reading: NA28 / UBS5 (both print the standard Greek reading with full apparatus noting the sys variant); the SBLGNT agrees and is equally reliable for this verse. Metzger's Textual Commentary (2nd ed., 1994) provides the definitive committee discussion at pp. 1–2.
assessment.open_questions: 1) Whether the Sinaitic Syriac reading at 1:16 reflects access to a pre-canonical or very early Greek Vorlage that has otherwise been lost, or whether it is entirely explicable as an internal Syriac scribal development — a question that bears on the broader history of the Syriac Gospel tradition and its independence from the Greek. 2) The relationship between the genealogical formula's deliberate break at v. 16 and the redactional theology of Matthew's infancy narrative: whether the passive construction was original to Matthew or was itself an early theological correction to a proto-Matthean source that may have had a different formulation — a question that intersects source criticism with textual criticism but cannot be resolved by manuscript evidence alone.

_validation.confidence_note: The core text-critical analysis is sound and reflects mainstream scholarship, but several specific manuscript attributions and Metzger citation details contain inaccuracies or overstatements.

flagged_claims.claim: Metzger's Textual Commentary (2nd ed., 1994) provides the definitive committee discussion at pp. 1–2
flagged_claims.reason: Specific page references should be verified; while Matt 1:16 is discussed early in the commentary, the exact pagination claim is precise and could be incorrect. Also, Metzger's discussion of Matt 1:16 actually focuses more on the variant reading involving 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, begat Jesus' as found in some manuscripts—not exclusively sys.

The UBS rating for Matt 1:16 in Metzger's commentary is debatable here; the committee actually addresses multiple variant forms at this verse (including Greek minuscule variants like Θ f13 reading 'Joseph, to whom being betrothed Mary the virgin bore Jesus'). The rating and the framing as primarily a sys-driven issue understates the Greek variant tradition.

flagged_claims.claim: Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin manuscripts show minor orthographic or stylistic variations
flagged_claims.reason: D is actually lacunose for much of Matthew 1; its testimony at 1:16 should be verified rather than vaguely characterized.

flagged_claims.claim: f13 ... offer no support for the sys variant and present the received text without notable divergence
flagged_claims.reason: This is factually questionable. Family 13 (and Θ) are commonly cited as supporting a distinctive Greek variant at Matt 1:16 reading something like 'Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, begot Jesus'—the very type of reading associated with sys. The analysis incorrectly places f13 with the received text.
P66 is a papyrus of the Gospel of John, not Matthew. Listing it as an Alexandrian witness for Matthew (even noting non-extant) is a category error.

flagged_claims.claim: interpreted by some scholars (e.g., Burkitt) as preserving an archaic pre-theological tradition
flagged_claims.reason: Burkitt's actual position on sys at Matt 1:16 was more nuanced; he did not simply argue it preserved a pre-theological adoptionist tradition. The attribution risks oversimplification.

flagged_claims.claim: Curetonian Syriac (syc) reading: ... 'she bore to him Jesus who is called the Christ'
flagged_claims.reason: The exact wording of syc at Matt 1:16 should be verified; the description as an 'intermediate form' may not accurately reflect its actual reading, which in standard editions is closer to the Greek standard text.

flagged_claims.claim: a conclusion that has not been seriously challenged in critical scholarship since the early twentieth century debates around Burkitt's proposals
flagged_claims.reason: Overstatement; the sys variant continues to be discussed in scholarship (e.g., by Klijn, Petersen, and others) well beyond the early 20th century.

safe_claims: The SBLGNT, NA28, and UBS5 agree on the standard Greek reading at Matt 1:16
The Sinaitic Syriac (sys) contains a notable variant at this verse
The Greek tradition uses passive ἐγεννήθη at v.16, breaking the active ἐγέννησεν pattern of vv. 2–15
א and B support the standard reading
The Byzantine/Majority Text agrees with the Alexandrian witnesses here
The variant has been discussed in connection with the virginal conception tradition
